course.title: Cell Biology Basics (tutor eval)
course.description: A short introduction to how cells are built, how they move materials, how they get energy, how enzymes work, and how cells divide.
course.learning_objectives: Describe the main organelles and what each one does. Explain diffusion, osmosis and active transport. Compare photosynthesis and cellular respiration. Explain how enzymes speed up reactions. Compare mitosis and meiosis.
course.prerequisites: Basic high-school chemistry: atoms, molecules, and chemical reactions. No previous biology course is required.

sessions.title: Lesson 1: Cell structure
sessions.description:
Every cell is surrounded by a cell membrane, a phospholipid bilayer that controls what enters and leaves the cell.

The nucleus contains the cell's DNA and controls the cell's activities. Ribosomes read messenger RNA and build proteins; some float in the cytoplasm and others sit on the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins for transport.

Mitochondria are the site of most cellular respiration. Plant cells also have chloroplasts, where photosynthesis happens, and a rigid cell wall made of cellulose outside the membrane.

sessions.title: Lesson 2: Moving materials across membranes
sessions.description:
Diffusion is the net movement of particles from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration. It needs no energy from the cell.

Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane, toward the side with the higher solute concentration. An animal cell placed in a hypotonic solution takes in water and swells, and may burst. In a hypertonic solution it loses water and shrivels.

Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient and uses energy from ATP. The sodium-potassium pump moves three sodium ions out of the cell and two potassium ions into the cell for each ATP it uses.

sessions.title: Lesson 3: Photosynthesis
sessions.description:
Photosynthesis turns light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose. It takes place in chloroplasts.

The light-dependent reactions happen in the thylakoid membranes. Chlorophyll absorbs light, water molecules are split, and oxygen is released as a by-product. These reactions produce ATP and NADPH.

The Calvin cycle takes place in the stroma, the fluid around the thylakoids. It uses ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to fix carbon dioxide into sugar.

sessions.title: Lesson 4: Cellular respiration
sessions.description:
Cellular respiration releases the energy stored in glucose and captures it as ATP.

Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm. It splits one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules and produces a net gain of two ATP. It does not need oxygen.

The Krebs cycle takes place in the mitochondrial matrix and releases carbon dioxide. The electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane produces most of the ATP, about 34 molecules per glucose. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and combines with hydrogen to form water.

Without oxygen, cells use fermentation. Muscle cells produce lactic acid, and yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

sessions.title: Lesson 5: Enzymes
sessions.description:
Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts: they speed up chemical reactions by lowering the activation energy, and they are not used up in the reaction.

The substrate binds to the enzyme's active site, which has a specific shape. High temperature or an extreme pH changes the shape of the active site, so the enzyme is denatured and stops working.

A competitive inhibitor is a molecule that binds to the active site and blocks the substrate.

sessions.title: Lesson 6: Cell division
sessions.description:
Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells, used for growth and repair. Its phases, in order, are prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, followed by cytokinesis, which divides the cytoplasm.

Meiosis produces gametes. It involves two divisions and halves the chromosome number, so the resulting cells are haploid.

During meiosis, crossing over happens when homologous chromosomes exchange segments of DNA. This increases genetic variation.
